Over $2 billion in additional crypto liquidations occurred over the weekend; the Fear & Greed Index collapsed to 10 — 'Extreme Fear' — the lowest reading of 2026. Traditional commodities closed Friday mixed: gold $3,888 (down 4.7% for the week — steepest weekly loss of 2026), silver at a one-year low of $48.65, Brent $95.84, WTI $88.56. Newcastle coal firmed to ~$146. Dollar index 103.4 (19-month high); 10-year yield above 5.15%. APEC Shenzhen November 18–19 provides a Trump–Xi meeting that could address the November 27 gallium/germanium/antimony deadline — now 11 days away. Anthropic prices Wednesday at $70–$78 per share (~$1T valuation, down from $2T); trading Thursday under ANT. Hormuz attacks persist — at least five incidents in November's first two weeks.

overview: The weekend was defined by Bitcoin's ongoing collapse, which deepened Friday's losses and sent the cryptocurrency to $62,112 on Sunday — its weakest level since July and more than 50% below its October 2025 all-time high of $126,080. Over $2 billion in additional crypto liquidations occurred over the weekend, bringing the two-week total above $4 billion as thin weekend liquidity amplified the downturn. The Fear and Greed Index collapsed to 10 — the lowest reading of 2026 — as nearly 90% of weekend liquidations hit long positions. Ethereum touched $1,718 before recovering to approximately $1,834, down more than 60% from its August 2025 all-time high. MARA disclosed it had sold 13,597 BTC (approximately $1.1 billion) over six weeks, while MSCI confirmed it will remove Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) from global standard indexes effective November 30, threatening forced selling of the largest corporate Bitcoin holder's shares. Combined stablecoin supply (USDT, USDC and DAI) has fallen $11.5 billion over 30 days — a record contraction — draining buying capacity from the crypto ecosystem. CME FedWatch prices approximately 88.5% odds of a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC and 11.5% for a 50-basis-point move, after Fed Governor Christopher Waller floated a half-point increase. Traditional commodities closed Friday mixed: gold settled near $3,888, down 4.7% for the week — its steepest weekly loss of 2026 — while silver held at a one-year low of $48.65. Brent crude was essentially flat at $95.84, with WTI at $88.56. The dollar index remained near 103.4, a 19-month high, and the 10-year Treasury yield held above 5.15%.

The week ahead is extraordinarily dense with catalysts. APEC leaders convene in Shenzhen on November 18–19, providing a Trump–Xi meeting that could address the November 27 deadline for China's suspended US-specific ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports — now 11 days away. The broader Busan truce was extended to January 10, but the specific export-control suspensions have their own legal deadlines, and neither government had published notices to extend the November 10 and November 27 dates as of late October. Anthropic is set to price its IPO on Wednesday at $70–$78 per share — implying a valuation of approximately $916 billion to $1 trillion, well below the nearly $2 trillion discussed in early autumn — with trading under ticker ANT on Thursday. Orders are reportedly six times oversubscribed, and a seven-way chip-and-cloud private placement (Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners) adds $26 billion of Class N shares. Hormuz attacks persisted into November with at least five incidents in the first two weeks, including a VLCC engine-room strike, a tanker set ablaze off Oman and a US strike on a sanctions-busting cargo vessel; oil spills from damaged tankers have reached the shores of Oman and the UAE. Newcastle coal firmed to approximately $146, supported by LNG tightness and approaching winter demand. LME base metals remained under pressure from the dollar surge, with nickel falling to $15,905 and copper easing to $6.07 per pound ($13,375 per tonne), while tin outperformed at $46,897 on tight inventory. The broader risk environment remains hostile for non-yielding and speculative assets, with yields above 5%, a dollar near 20-month highs and contracting stablecoin supply continuing to drain liquidity.

watchItems.title: Bitcoin crashes to $62,112 over the weekend — lowest since July, $4 billion liquidated in two weeks
watchItems.text: Bitcoin's collapse accelerated through the weekend, plunging from Friday's $68,300 to a low of $62,112 on Sunday — its weakest level since early July and more than 50% below its October 2025 all-time high of $126,080. Over $2 billion in additional crypto liquidations occurred over Saturday and Sunday, with nearly 90% hitting long positions, bringing the two-week total above $4 billion. The Fear and Greed Index collapsed to 10 — 'Extreme Fear' — the lowest reading since the January 2026 deleveraging crisis. Bitcoin recovered to approximately $65,000 by Sunday night but remains deeply below its 200-week moving average near $68,000. Coinbase Institutional identifies support zones at $62,000, then $58,566 (the July 2026 annual low). MARA disclosed it sold 13,597 BTC (approximately $1.1 billion) over six weeks and said it will continue selling. MSCI's removal of Strategy from global standard indexes effective November 30 could force index funds to sell the largest corporate Bitcoin holder. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $1.07 billion in net outflows during November 9–13, including $908 million from BlackRock's IBIT. Stablecoin supply (USDT, USDC and DAI combined) has fallen $11.5 billion over 30 days, a record contraction that reduces crypto buying capacity.

watchItems.title: APEC Shenzhen November 18–19 — Trump–Xi meeting could shape critical minerals and trade policy
watchItems.text: APEC leaders convene in Shenzhen on November 18–19, providing the last major diplomatic window before the November 27 deadline when China's suspended US-specific ban on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials exports is set to resume. The broader Busan trade truce was extended to January 10, 2027, but the specific export-control suspensions have their own legal deadlines — and neither government had published notices to extend the November 10 or November 27 dates as of late October. The November 10 deadline for China's broader October 2025 controls (covering five heavy rare earths, rare-earth equipment, lithium batteries and graphite anode material) has already passed with no confirmed extension. Gallium remains at approximately $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus $460 domestically — a roughly 4.5x premium. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. The APEC timing coincides with Anthropic's IPO pricing on Wednesday, creating an unusual alignment of geopolitical and technology catalysts.

watchItems.title: Anthropic IPO prices Wednesday at $70–$78 per share — valuation revised to approximately $1 trillion
watchItems.text: Anthropic is set to price its IPO on Wednesday, November 18, and begin trading on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19. The offering of 825 million Class A shares at $70–$78 per share implies a valuation of approximately $916 billion to $1.02 trillion — significantly below the nearly $2 trillion discussed in early autumn. Orders are reportedly six times oversubscribed. A separate private placement sees seven chip-and-cloud suppliers — Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners — buying $26 billion of non-voting Class N shares at the IPO price, bringing the total raise to approximately $90 billion. Analysts have cited the IPO as one factor draining liquidity from crypto markets, as institutional investors sell liquid risk assets to fund allocations. The listing comes during a difficult week for tech, with the Nasdaq in a technical correction (down more than 10% from its peak) and Nvidia still reeling from Jensen Huang's resignation.

watchItems.title: November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline now 11 days away
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline — when China's one-year suspension of its US-specific export prohibition on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials expires — is now 11 days away. The broader trade truce extension to January 10 does not automatically cover these material-specific suspensions, which have their own legal instruments. The November 10 deadline for China's broader October 2025 controls has already passed without a published extension. APEC in Shenzhen this week provides a narrow window for a Trump–Xi discussion. China produces about 98% of global gallium and dominates germanium and antimony supply. Ex-China prices remain at steep premiums: gallium at $2,100 per kilogram (4.5x China domestic), tungsten APT at $2,725 per mtu in Rotterdam (3.5x Chinese FOB). If the bans resume, Western semiconductor, defence and advanced-materials industries face renewed supply disruption.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Down 4.7% for the week — steepest weekly loss of 2026 · 10Y yield 5.15% · dollar 103.4 · Waller floats 50bp hike
desk.sum: Gold settled near $3,888 per ounce on Friday, up 0.3% on the day but posting its steepest weekly decline of 2026 at approximately 4.7%. The weekly low of $3,856.7 marked a fresh 20-week low. The October PPI (0.3% MoM, 6.5% YoY) was slightly below consensus but failed to shift rate-hike expectations — CME FedWatch now prices 88.5% odds of a 25-basis-point hike and 11.5% for 50 basis points at the December 8–9 FOMC after Fed Governor Waller floated a half-point increase. The 10-year Treasury yield held above 5.15% and the dollar index remained at 103.4, a 19-month high. APEC in Shenzhen this week could provide clarity on trade and tariff policy. Central bank buying at 675 tonnes year to date remains supportive but insufficient to offset the yield and dollar headwinds.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: One-year low · gold-silver ratio ~80 · down 17%+ over the past month · $50 support lost
desk.sum: Silver held at $48.65 per ounce — a one-year low — after plunging 2.6% on Friday and losing the psychologically important $50 level. The gold-to-silver ratio remains elevated near 80 as silver's dual precious-industrial profile continues to work against it: rising yields reduce precious-metal appeal while weakening tech sentiment undermines industrial demand. Silver has now fallen more than 17% over the past month. Solar panel demand provides a structural floor but with the 10-year above 5.15%, the dollar at a 19-month high and the Nasdaq in a technical correction, silver remains the most vulnerable precious metal. The APEC summit this week and Anthropic IPO pricing add to near-term uncertainty.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $88.56 · second straight weekly loss ~2.5% · 37 ship attacks in Oct · OPEC+ output rising · IEA sees surplus in Q4
desk.sum: Brent crude settled essentially flat at $95.84 per barrel on Friday, posting a second consecutive weekly decline of approximately 2.5%. WTI settled at $88.56, down 0.2%. The weekly loss was driven by growing supply surplus concerns — OPEC+ October output rose, led by Saudi Arabia — and rising US crude and fuel inventories that signalled softer domestic demand. Brent hit a two-month low of $91.49 on Tuesday before recovering on Thursday after unconfirmed Houthi claims of attacks on Saudi oil sites. Hormuz attacks persist, with at least five incidents in November's first two weeks. A Qatari-brokered Iranian proposal to reopen Hormuz briefly sent Brent down 3.6% on November 9 before Trump reiterated the US does not need a deal with Iran. The IEA expects the oil market to return to surplus in Q4.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$13,375/t · 4-month low · LME stocks rose to ~320,000t from 205,000t in Aug · dollar 103.4
desk.sum: Copper eased to $6.07 per pound (approximately $13,375 per tonne LME), down 1.5% on Friday, sitting at its weakest level in four months. LME inventories have risen to approximately 320,000 tonnes from around 205,000 tonnes in August, easing the supply tightness narrative. The dollar index at 103.4 makes dollar-denominated commodities more expensive for non-US buyers. Physical supply in China remains tight, with import premiums at record levels and smelters cutting output, but the macro headwind from yields above 5% and the surging dollar continues to overpower the constructive supply picture. AI data-centre and electrification demand remains a structural long-term driver, but higher borrowing costs for infrastructure firms weigh on near-term sentiment.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up ~42% YTD · LNG JKM ~$32 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · winter demand approaching · Hormuz traffic 65% below pre-war
desk.sum: Newcastle coal firmed to approximately $146 per tonne, up from $143 earlier in the week, as the broader energy complex remained supported. Coal is up approximately 42% year to date as the Hormuz gas shock continues to revive thermal coal demand. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of LNG supply offline. The IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3% — the steepest annual drop on record. Hormuz shipping traffic is approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels even as Gulf oil exports partially recover. EU storage sits below the five-year average ahead of winter. The combination of LNG supply tightness, winter demand approaching and geopolitical risk continues to provide a firm floor for seaborne coal pricing.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Eased from 3-week high · EV shift weighs on auto catalyst demand · hydrogen electrolysis provides floor
desk.sum: Platinum fell to approximately $1,500 per ounce on Friday, under pressure from the hawkish rate environment and the stronger dollar. Platinum eased from a three-week high earlier in the week as stronger-than-expected US inflation and jobs data raised expectations of another Fed rate hike. Higher borrowing costs, weaker vehicle production and the shift to EVs continue to weigh on automotive catalyst demand — platinum's largest end market. Expectations of a modest market surplus add bearish pressure. Support comes from rising hybrid production, continued catalytic-converter demand, and longer-term interest in green hydrogen electrolysis. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Sitting just above $1,000 psychological support · EV transition headwind persists · down ~28% YoY
desk.sum: Palladium eased to $1,002 per ounce, sitting just above the psychologically important $1,000 support level and down approximately 28% year-over-year. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — remains the dominant longer-term dynamic. A decisive break below $1,000 would be technically significant and could trigger stop-loss selling. With yields above 5%, the dollar at a 19-month high and the macro environment hostile to precious metals, palladium's profile remains challenging. Some support comes from tight supply at South African mines and potential substitution demand from platinum users.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: 37 ships attacked in Oct · at least 5 incidents in Nov's first 2 weeks · 130 total since Feb · oil spills reaching Oman/UAE shores · traffic 65% below pre-war
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz risk remained critical with at least five new incidents in November's first two weeks adding to October's record 37 ship attacks. On November 7, US aircraft disabled a cargo vessel that had visited an Iranian port. On November 8, a Navig8 tanker was set ablaze off Oman, with oil slicks reaching Omani shores; two more tankers were hit the same day. On November 10, UKMTO reported another tanker struck northeast of Oman. On November 11, Iran reportedly targeted ship navigation systems on an Omani island. An LNG carrier operated by Qatar's Nakilat was also struck on October 30 south of Iran's Lavan Island — prompting Qatar to reserve the right to take 'necessary measures under international law.' Hormuz shipping traffic is approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. The International Maritime Organisation has confirmed 130 incidents since late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed. Despite the escalation, crude prices hit two-month lows on November 10 before partially recovering.
desk.src: Baird Maritime · gCaptain · UKMTO · Seatrade Maritime

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Rebounded from Thursday's selloff · dollar headwind persists · WASDE tighter balance sheets still supportive
desk.sum: December corn settled at 446¢ per bushel on Friday, up 0.8%, recovering part of Thursday's selloff in a broad grain bounce. The rebound came despite the dollar index at a 19-month high, suggesting end-of-week short-covering. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from last week's WASDE report continues to provide structural support, with the November yield cut (179.6 bushels per acre) below all analyst estimates. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions. The weekly performance remains negative despite Friday's bounce, with the hawkish rates environment and strong dollar capping upside potential for US grain export competitiveness.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Recovered from Thursday's reversal · SovEcon: Russian exports 36 mmt vs USDA 39 mmt · Abu Dhabi grain corridor talks key risk
desk.sum: December wheat settled at 593½¢ per bushel on Friday, up 1.6%, recovering a significant portion of Thursday's 15¼-cent selloff. The rebound brought wheat back within range of the 600¢ level. SovEcon's cut of its Russian wheat export estimate to 36 million tonnes (below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast) remains a medium-term bullish factor. The Abu Dhabi grain corridor talks remain a key potential bearish catalyst if they restart stalled Black Sea shipments. Despite Friday's bounce, wheat posted a weekly loss as the macro-driven selling on Wednesday and Thursday overwhelmed the WASDE-driven rally. The stronger dollar continues to weigh on US export competitiveness.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month $12.33 · rebounded from Thursday · stronger dollar still weighing on export competitiveness
desk.sum: January soybeans settled at $12.33 per bushel (1,233¢) on Friday, up 1.2%, bouncing back from Thursday's decline. The rebound was supported by end-of-week short-covering despite the dollar's surge to a 19-month high. South American supplies remain more competitive than US offerings at current exchange rates, and Chinese buying interest is still muted. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the WASDE report provides a structural floor. The Busan truce extension to January 10 ensures China's commitment to purchase at least 25 million tonnes of US soybeans per year through 2028 remains intact.

desk.m: ETH $1,834 · crashed to $62,112 Sun low · $4B+ liquidated in 2 weeks · Fear & Greed at 10 · MARA sold 13,597 BTC · Strategy MSCI removal Nov 30

The cryptocurrency recovered to approximately $65,000 by Sunday night. Over $2 billion in additional liquidations occurred over the weekend, with nearly 90% hitting long positions. The Fear and Greed Index collapsed to 10 — the lowest reading of 2026. Ethereum touched $1,718 before recovering to approximately $1,834. CME FedWatch prices 88.5% odds of a 25bp December hike and 11.5% for 50bp.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM ~$32 · TTF fell ~18% to $28 · HH $3.00 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · LNG carrier attacked Oct 30
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) trades near $32 per MMBtu, holding steady as winter demand approaches. European TTF fell to approximately $28 per MMBtu, down about 18% week-over-week on easing near-term supply concerns, while Henry Hub rose modestly to $3.00. The October 30 attack on a Nakilat LNG carrier south of Iran's Lavan Island marked an escalation in Hormuz hostilities, with Qatar reserving the right to 'necessary measures under international law.' QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of supply offline. The IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3%. EU storage sits at 73%, below the five-year average ahead of winter.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · Hormuz attacks persist — 5+ incidents in Nov · oil spills reaching Oman/UAE shores · 11 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. Hormuz attacks persisted into November with at least five incidents in the first two weeks, including a tanker set ablaze off Oman with oil slicks reaching the shores of Oman and the UAE — further reducing the near-term probability of Middle Eastern supply resumption. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Chinese domestic sulfur holds near 7,200 yuan per tonne. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 11 days away. APEC in Shenzhen this week provides a diplomatic window, but Trump's reiterated stance that Washington does not need a deal with Iran signals a continued hardline posture.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · grain rebound Friday modestly supportive · Busan truce soybean commitment intact
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Friday's grain rebound modestly improved fertiliser sentiment, though the weekly performance remains negative for grains. The Busan trade truce extension to January 10 ensures China's soybean purchase commitments remain intact, supporting underlying grain demand. The WASDE-driven tighter grain balance sheets remain supportive for the 2027 planting season. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 11 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · APEC Shenzhen Nov 18–19 · Busan truce extended but specific bans have own deadlines
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The critical near-term catalyst is the November 27 deadline — now 11 days away — when the suspension of China's US-specific export prohibition on antimony (and gallium, germanium, superhard materials) is set to expire. The broader Busan trade truce was extended to January 10, but the specific export-control suspensions have their own legal instruments that require separate notices to extend. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, providing the last major diplomatic window. The November 10 deadline for Announcement No. 70's broader controls has already passed without a published extension.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 11 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · Ge 29,750 CNY/kg · Alcoa Wagerup FID but not producing
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium for ex-China supply. Germanium in China sits at approximately 29,750 yuan per kilogram, up about 9% on the month and over 113% year-over-year. The November 27 deadline is now 11 days away. APEC in Shenzhen this week provides the last major diplomatic window before the deadline, where Trump and Xi could discuss critical mineral supply alongside the broader trade truce. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. China produces about 98% of global gallium.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Firmer at $5.30 vs recent $5.02 · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ supply
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, up from recent levels near $5.02. The modest recovery reflects stabilisation in steel demand rather than a structural shift. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The November 27 export-control deadline could impact vanadium indirectly if superhard materials restrictions affect adjacent supply chains.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Recovered from $4,700 four-month low · Sodexam: Ivory Coast output may fall 21–25% · El Niño 'exceptionally strong' · ICE inventories at 2.5-year high
desk.sum: ICE cocoa settled near $5,267 per tonne on Friday, continuing its recovery from four-month lows near $4,700 touched earlier in the week. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projected 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event' shortening the rainy season. Reuters projected the mid-crop could fall 42–50% to 300,000–350,000 tonnes. Harmattan wind risk in December–January adds further supply concern. ICE warehouse inventories remain elevated at a 2.5-year high of 3,751,670 bags, capping the near-term recovery. Heavy rains reportedly damaged roads in key growing regions, slowing bean deliveries. Subdued chocolate demand has contributed to rising exchange stocks.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Down ~31% YoY · Glencore wins $900M US stockpile contract · Rotterdam $17–18/lb · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds near $33,525 per tonne, down approximately 31% year-over-year and under continued pressure from the EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP. Glencore reportedly won a US government contract to supply up to $900 million of cobalt over five years for strategic stockpiles. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $17–18 per pound. The DRC maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027. Antaike expects recycled cobalt supply to rise 26% to 50,000 tonnes this year. The structural reduction in cobalt intensity per battery continues to weigh on the medium-term demand outlook.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Near one-year low · SMM: Chinese stockpile 175k t · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028 · new mine restarts adding supply
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures hover near ¥90,650 per tonne, close to a one-year low. SMM's revised inventory estimate of 175,000 tonnes in Chinese stockpiles remains a bearish overhang. Mineral Resources restarted Bald Hill and Core Lithium restarted Finniss, adding to supply. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. Lithium's inability to rally despite the broader commodity complex finding some support underscores the structural oversupply challenge. The Busan truce soybean and trade commitments have no direct lithium impact.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil above $95 supports synthetic rubber costs
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Oil remaining above $95 modestly supports synthetic rubber costs, which indirectly benefits natural rubber pricing. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The stronger dollar at a 19-month high is a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Futures near 9-month high above $91 · long-term contracts near $99/lb · IAEA raises nuclear capacity outlook · 78 reactors under construction
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds at approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, with futures hovering near a nine-month high. Long-term contract prices continue climbing near record US levels of $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. The IAEA raised its outlook for global nuclear capacity over the next two decades and counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide. Kazatomprom reported 25% year-over-year growth in sales turnover for the September quarter, driven by higher sales volumes and a 17% rise in realised prices. Delays at Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements. Italy is considering a legal framework to restore nuclear power.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: China rare earth index fell to 254.7 in Nov · ex-China premiums up to 10x · Nov 10 broader controls deadline passed · Nov 27 US-specific deadline ahead
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, softening, as the China Rare Earth Industry Association price index fell to 254.7 by early November from a peak of 310 in April. Western buyers face premiums of up to 10x Chinese prices for heavy rare earths. The November 10 deadline for the broader October 2025 controls (covering five heavy rare earths, equipment, lithium batteries and graphite) has passed without a published extension. The November 27 US-specific deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony adds further uncertainty. LS Cable & System and KMMI committed $490 million to reduce reliance on Chinese rare earth magnets. Lynas' Malaysian plant maintenance shutdown continues.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners are holding a firm pricing stance, with Comilog (Gabonese lumps) at $4.50 per mtu and Consolidated Minerals (Australian 46% lumps) at $4.80 per mtu for recent shipments. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption limits gains.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Fell sharply on dollar strength · up 2.4% MoM but weak · Indonesia RKAB quota tightening provides some support · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel fell to $15,905 per tonne on Friday, down 1.9%, pressured by the dollar index at 103.4 — a 19-month high. The decline was sharper than the broader base metals complex, with nickel underperforming copper and tin. Indonesia's potential tightening of RKAB mining quotas provides a modest floor, but the global nickel surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. Nickel is up about 2.4% month-over-month but the macro environment remains hostile, with yields above 5.15% and the hawkish rate outlook capping industrial metal sentiment.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Best performer among base metals · LME backwardation widened to $715 (strongest since Jul 2023) · cancelled warrants 19.5% · Myanmar ban constraining supply
desk.sum: LME tin rose to $46,897 per tonne on Friday, up 0.5% — the best performer among base metals on the day. The LME spot-versus-3M backwardation widened to $715, the strongest since July 2023, signalling tightening near-term supply. Cancelled warrants remain elevated near 19.5%, suggesting further inventory drawdowns ahead. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. Tin's outperformance on a day when nickel fell 1.9% and copper dropped 1.5% reflects its significantly tighter fundamental supply position. SHFE tin closed at 348,850 yuan in the night session.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: TCs deeply negative · LME stocks ~142,625 mt · dollar pressure persistent · smelter curtailments continue
desk.sum: LME zinc eased to $3,703 per tonne on Friday, down 0.6%, with the dollar at a 19-month high continuing to weigh on the market. LME inventories have been falling, with stocks near 142,625 mt, continuing the drawdown trend. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments. SMM described off-season demand as weak across Chinese hubs, though limited supply in some regions supported premiums. The structural supply deficit that has driven zinc higher through 2026 remains intact, but the combination of yields above 5%, the dollar surge and soft downstream consumption is capping near-term upside. Zinc is up about 23% year-over-year despite recent weakness.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,725 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 11 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: European tungsten APT trades at $2,725 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu. Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. Chongyi tungsten enterprises raised long-term contract prices for the first half of November, reflecting upstream tightness. The November 27 deadline for the US-specific ban is now 11 days away. APEC in Shenzhen this week provides a diplomatic window. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls on tungsten processing technology.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · attacks persist in Nov · Nakilat LNG carrier struck Oct 30
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The October 30 attack on a Nakilat LNG carrier south of Iran's Lavan Island — Qatar's national fleet — marked a significant escalation. Qatar reserved the right to 'necessary measures under international law,' but so far no military response has materialised. Attacks persisting into November, combined with Trump's stance that Washington does not need a deal with Iran, further extend the timeline for Ras Laffan facility repairs, currently estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. Commercial inventories remain at their lowest since 2008.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · grain rebound modestly supportive
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Friday's grain rebound modestly improved the near-term fertiliser demand outlook. The Busan truce extension to January 10 preserves China's soybean purchase commitments, supporting underlying grain demand. The ongoing Hormuz attacks further reduce the probability of Middle Eastern sulfur supply normalising, keeping the cost structure elevated for phosphate producers.

quiz: Bitcoin crashed to $62,112 on Sunday — its lowest since July — with the Fear and Greed Index collapsing to 10 and over $2 billion in additional weekend liquidations, bringing the two-week total above $4 billion.
Gold surged 2% on Friday to close above $3,950 as investors fled crashing crypto markets and rotated into safe-haven assets.

Gold actually settled at $3,888, essentially flat on the day (+0.3%). Despite crypto's crash, the hawkish rate environment — yields above 5.15% and the dollar at a 19-month high — continued to cap gold, which posted its steepest weekly loss of 2026 at 4.7%.
APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen on November 18–19, coinciding with Anthropic's IPO pricing on Wednesday — aligning geopolitical and technology catalysts in the same week.
Brent crude rallied 4% to above $100 on Friday as new Hormuz attacks sank two tankers, with WTI surging above $92.

Brent actually settled essentially flat at $95.84 and posted a second consecutive weekly decline of about 2.5%. Despite ongoing Hormuz attacks, crude prices hit two-month lows earlier in the week as growing supply surplus and rising US inventories weighed on sentiment.
Anthropic's IPO price range was set at $70–$78 per share, implying a valuation of approximately $916 billion to $1.02 trillion — well below the nearly $2 trillion discussed in early autumn.
Nickel rallied 3% on Friday as Indonesia announced it would immediately halt all mining quota approvals, triggering a short-covering rally.

LME nickel actually FELL 1.9% to $15,905 per tonne, pressured by the dollar index at a 19-month high. Indonesia's potential RKAB tightening provides only modest support against the persistent global surplus.

The November 27 deadline — when China's suspension of its US-specific ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports expires — is now 11 days away, with neither government having published extension notices.
Newcastle coal fell 5% to $130 per tonne as mild winter forecasts and rising LNG supply eased energy demand concerns.

Newcastle coal actually FIRMED to approximately $146 per tonne, supported by continued LNG supply tightness from QatarEnergy's force majeure and approaching winter demand. Coal is up about 42% year to date.
